new_statements.quote: One of the most remarkable phonological traits of Lende is its system of tones. Unlike most Central Tibetan varieties or the tonal West(ern) Tibetan varieties, the Lende dialect does not show a binary tone distinction (high vs. low), but a ternary distinction (high, medium, low). Medium tone corresponds to originally voiced root consonants of Old Tibetan not preceded by any affix, low tone to originally voiced root consonants preceded by oral or nasal affixes.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Kyirong Tibetan as tonal (Hildebrandt 2007, reproducing Huber 2000: 22-24, six phonemic tones over three registers); Zeisler's ternary high/medium/low register description is the same type, and like the catalog's deciding source she records no stress rule. The catalog_records entry in the target has an empty rule field, consistent with a tonal coding without a stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The review presents Lende (Kyirong) Tibetan as a tone language with a three-way register contrast (high, medium, low) tied historically to the voicing and prefixation of Old Tibetan root consonants; it says nothing about word stress or accent (the words stress and accent do not occur anywhere in the review). The reviewer also states that Huber's treatment of phonology is well informed, which is indirect evidence that the grammar's phonology chapter did not give her anything on stress to report.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; on tone the reviewer notes that low tone bundles with breathy voice or prenasalisation (Huber p. 15 quoted) and questions whether voice or tone is the concomitant feature
new_statements.identity_note: Huber 2005 and Zeisler's review describe the Lende valley subdialect of Kyirong county (Tibet Autonomous Region, on the Nepal border), which Zeisler characterises as mixing Central Tibetan and West(ern) Tibetan features. The catalog entry is for Kyirong Tibetan as a whole; all held sources (Huber 2000, Huber 2005 via the review, Hildebrandt 2007) rest on Huber's Lende data.

sources.quote: All 18 Kyirong phonological-word domains (compiled by Hildebrandt from Huber's grammar and Hall & Hildebrandt 2008; DataSourceType 'Grammar Explicit/Implicit') are tone or segmental domains (contour-tone neutralization, tone defaults to H, deaspiration, voicing assimilation, cluster licensing...); CohesionPatternStressPresence = 'other' for every row, whereas the same database codes 'stress-related' domains for Lhasa Tibetan, Kham, Manange and Limbu. Indirect but pointed evidence that the primary descriptions state no word-stress domain.

Bibliographic only: confirms Hall & Hildebrandt 2008, Linguistics 46.2: 215-248, DOI 10.1515/LING.2008.010; no author PDF linked. 'Syllable and phonological word in two Tibetan dialects' (Glottolog ref 678182) does not appear in the CV publication list.
